39a

A row you can't tick

The last surface in the repo. Some closing lines aren't chores — they are receipts for work filed elsewhere, and they complete themselves. Everything about the row exists to say so before a closer reaches for it.

‹ Closing
Closing manager
Mon, Aug 11
Four rows on the closing list that the closer cannot tick. Each one completes itself when its source report is submitted — which is why the tick is green rather than the mustard every other completed row uses.
✓ AM Prep submitted ×18 Submitted by Marco Reyes at 6:12 AM Edit
✓ Opening verified Submitted by Ana Ruiz at 5:48 AM, updated by Marco Reyes at 6:31 AM
Mid-day prep submitted Pending — submit from the dashboard
Cash report signed Pending — submit from the dashboard
Row one carries an Edit link because the viewer is a key holder; row two is the same completed state without it. The link is deliberately a quiet text button rather than a button proper — editing a submitted report is a correction, not the row's purpose.
Both pending rows are inert, because read-only is a property of the closing, not of a row — and 38a establishes this Monday as auto-finalized and never submitted, so every row in it is read-only. While a closing is still open the same rows are tappable and go to their source page: opening to the opening page, mid-day to mid-day, cash to cash. The reason a row went unsubmitted lives in the Review section rather than inline, so the row stays a row.
Each destination is resolved from the row's own report type — opening to the opening page, mid-day to mid-day, cash to cash, and anything unrecognised falls back to AM Prep so a closer at 10pm lands somewhere real instead of a 404. That fallback exists because the route was once hardcoded to AM Prep and a first-shift smoke test found the misroute by tapping the opening row.
A green tick means “not by you”
Every other completed row on a closing list is mustard, tapped by the person standing there. These are green, and the source comment says why in as many words: so the closer immediately knows this came from a report, not a tap. A colour doing real semantic work — and the reason this could not be a branch inside the checklist row.
The fallback route is scar tissue
An unrecognised report type sends the closer to AM Prep rather than nowhere. That default exists because the route was once hardcoded to AM Prep and a first-shift smoke test caught the misroute when someone tapped the opening row. Worth keeping in the rebuild — and worth keeping the comment that explains it.
Attribution collapses a chain
One submitter reads “Submitted by Marco Reyes at 6:12 AM”. Two or more collapse into a chain through a shared formatter, so a report filed by one person and updated by another still fits on one line. The ARIA label switches strings to match, rather than reading a truncated version of the visible text.
Coverage closed
This was the last component in the repo without a frame. Every route and every substantial component is now drawn from source — 39 turns. What remains is the mobile pass's last two groups, a polish pass on the daily surfaces, and the build spec.
38a

The last checklist read back

One view serves opening, closing, AM prep and mid-day, and it has the hardest job of the three detail pages: a checklist line can be a tick, a temperature, a yes-or-no question or a paragraph, and they all arrive in the same shape.

‹ Reports

Two of the six stations, six of the twenty lines — the real page renders every one.

Marco Reyes
Note: Door seal is dragging — worth a look before it starts costing us degrees.
Photo

Luis Torres

The status prints as auto_finalized because that is what the component renders — its status map has no entry for it, so it falls back to the raw database value even though the translation exists. 3a shows the same report with the human label. A tick and a dash, nothing more — reports.detail.done is literally “✓” and not_done is an em dash. Skipped items are counted in the signal line but look identical to undone ones in the list, which is the one place this view loses information the closer had.
Readings sit above the stations on purpose, so a temperature is the first thing on the page rather than the fourteenth line of a station — and when one is out of range it takes the cta tone here and adds a clause to the signal line above. This report's temps are clean, which is what its row in the hub says too. And a yes-or-no line is deliberately excluded from that block: it stores its answer as a 0 or 1 in the same column a temperature uses, so including them would print “Bathroom stocked? 1” as a reading.
Three kinds of answer, one column. A question line renders Yes ✓ or No ✗; a free-text line renders its text as the answer and then suppresses its own note, because for that line the note is the answer. Count lines print the number. All three come out of one interpreter rather than three branches in the view.
The photo link is visible to anyone who can open the report — unlike the notes, which the loader nulls below level 5. So a low-level viewer sees that a reading was photographed but not what the closer wrote about it.
One column holds three kinds of answer
A yes-or-no line stores 0 or 1 in the same count_value a temperature uses, and a free-text line stores its answer in the note field. One interpreter untangles all three, so the view has no answer logic of its own — and the readings block has to exclude question lines explicitly, or it would print “Bathroom stocked? 1”.
A free-text answer is L5-gated by accident of storage
Because that answer lives in the note field, the loader's note redaction applies to it too — so below level 5 the question renders with no answer rather than with a hidden one. Correct outcome, reached indirectly. Worth stating in the spec so a rebuild doesn't separate the two and quietly expose it.
Skipped and undone look identical
The signal line counts them separately — 18/20 done, 1 skipped — but every incomplete line in the list shows the same em dash. The distinction the closer made is in the data and not on the page; a second glyph would recover it.
Photos are ungated, notes are not
The attached-photo link renders for any viewer of the report while the note beside it is nulled below level 5. So a key holder can open the photograph of a temperature log but cannot read what the closer wrote about it — deliberate per the source comment, and worth confirming that is still the intent.
Two statuses render untranslated
The view's status map covers only open, in progress, submitted and confirmed, and falls back to the raw column value for anything else — so an auto-finalized closing shows auto_finalized and an incomplete confirmation shows incomplete_confirmed. Both strings already exist in the translation file and the reports list already prints them properly. Two map entries, and it is the report a manager opens after an unfinished night.
Coverage after this turn
One surface remained after this turn — ReportReferenceItem — and 39a has since drawn it. That card is the current answer — the still-owed lists in 37a, 36a and 35a are dated history from before their turns landed, and the index at the top of the document agrees with this one.

Where prep lines come from

Two template-builder surfaces, and together they explain a rule the app takes seriously: prep is edited in exactly one place. The form on the left creates a line; the panel on the right can only describe them and point at the editor that owns them.

Two checkboxes appear conditionally and neither is cosmetic. Include a note field only exists when the section is Misc — which is why 33a's Cook bacon row has a note and the other three don't. Pick any other section and the option disappears rather than sitting there disabled.
Also create an Opening verification item shows only on AM Prep, and it defaults to on — adding a prep line quietly adds a second line to a different checklist unless someone unticks it. That is the right default and the least obvious thing on this form; it deserves a sentence of help text it does not have.
The type picker above is my addition. A new line is not shapeless without it — the server composes the columns from the section's shape plus the note checkbox, so a line always arrives matching whatever its section already is. What you cannot do is create a line that differs from its section, which is precisely what a mixed section is made of. Par and Unit are both optional — the unit dropdown opens on an em dash. A yes-or-no line has no par, so leaving them blank is the normal case for Misc, not an omission. Every new line is created required, at role level 3, with no way to change either here.

Collapsed by default, because a closing template is what you came here to edit and this is a neighbour's list. Opened, it is a summary with no edit affordances at all — every fix is a link out to the prep editor. Prep evolves in its own editor and is never publish-versioned with the closing and opening templates, so folding an editor in here would create two places to change one thing.
Its findings are advisory and stay out of the builder's Doctor totals for the same reason: they are not this template's problems. The badge counts them separately — five to review, from two unlinked lines, two missing Spanish, and one input-type difference.
The drift finding is the interesting one. The same line asks for a portion at one shop and a count at the other, which means the two locations' prep sheets are quietly not comparable. Nothing enforces agreement; the panel just says so and points at the editor.
Adding one line can create two
On AM Prep, “Also create an Opening verification item” defaults to ON — so a new prep line silently gains a matching line on the opening checklist unless someone unticks it. It is the right default and the least visible decision on the form; it needs help text explaining what the mirrored item is for.
The note field is section-conditional
It only appears when the section is Misc, which is exactly why 33a's Cook bacon row can carry a note and its three siblings cannot. The option vanishes for other sections rather than sitting disabled — worth keeping, and worth stating so nobody “fixes” it into a permanent field.
One editor per thing, enforced by omission
The overview panel has zero edit affordances and its findings stay out of the builder's Doctor totals. Prep is never publish-versioned alongside closing and opening, so a second editor here would mean two places to change one line. The restraint is the design.
Input-type drift is visible and unenforced
The same prep line can ask for a portion at one shop and a count at the other, which quietly makes the two locations' prep sheets incomparable. Nothing prevents it; the panel names it and links out. Deciding whether that should ever be allowed is a product question for the spec, not a bug.
Coverage after this turn
Two surfaces remained when this turn landed: ChecklistReportDetail and ReportReferenceItem. 38a has since built the first, so the current answer lives in 38a's card and in the index — this one is history.
A mixed section cannot be built here
The POST body carries no input type, and it does not need one: addPrepItem derives the columns as shapeToColumns(section.shape, includeNote). So every line created here inherits its section's shape — and a section like 33a's Catering station, which holds a count, a toggle and a text question, is unbuildable from this form. Each line has to be created and then converted one at a time through a separate per-line input-type route. The picker would let the exception be stated at creation instead.

Reading a shift back

Two of the pages behind 3a's report rows. Both are pure views: every gate lives in the loader, so a field the viewer isn't allowed to read arrives as null and simply has nothing to render. That is why the same page is safe for a key holder and a GM.

Six figures and the arithmetic between them is all visible: drawer minus float is the deposit, deposit against projected is the over. This is the same drawer 22a counts, read back a day later — and the report can afford to show every step because nobody is typing here.
The over-short note is null below level 5, and the redaction happens in the loader — this view never receives the string, so there is no field to leak. That is the pattern worth copying: don't render-gate a secret, don't send it.
Over renders green and short renders red, and an exact drawer reads simply “even”. Cents are formatted by hand here rather than through the money helper, which is why a zero-cent figure prints as $200.00 and not $200 — consistent, if verbose.

Marco's gradients and area-to-improve are the same record 9a shows him about himself — one record, two audiences. What he cannot see is the line beneath it: Note (managers only), which the loader strips entirely for an employee and for anyone below level 5.
Each dimension sums to two, because two evaluations were filed — the tally is derived from the same list below it, and counts only what this viewer was already allowed to open, so it can never become a side channel revealing a hidden one. Luis has no area to improve and no note, so neither block renders — an absent field rather than an empty one.
Shift activity omits anything overdue on purpose: on a report from last Tuesday, “overdue” would be a statement about today. Closing simply reads Not started, which is the truth about that night.
Redaction happens in the loader, never in the view
The cash over-short note and the manager-only eval note are both null by the time they reach these components. There is no conditional hiding a value that was sent anyway — the value was never sent. It is the strongest pattern in the reporting layer and the spec should state it as the house rule for anything role-scoped.
One record, two audiences
Marco's area-to-improve is the identical sentence 9a shows him about himself. The manager's view adds a private note beneath it that he will never see. Worth stating plainly in the handoff: the eval has a public half and a private half, and the split is enforced server-side.
The tally can't become a side channel
Per-dimension great/good/needs-work counts are computed only from the evals the viewer could already open, so an employee can never infer the existence of a hidden evaluation from a count that doesn't add up. Small decision, easy to get wrong in a rebuild.
Still owed at the time (two surfaces)
ChecklistReportDetail (the third hub detail view, and the largest) and ReportReferenceItem. Both are read-and-draw with no open questions. The two template-builder surfaces this card originally also named were built in 37a, above.
35a

Two modals I kept citing

A fifth scan caught these: surfaces I described in prose across ten sections without ever drawing. The step-up modal gates almost every irreversible action in the app, and the revoke modal is the only place a prepper explains undoing something. Both are decided by the server, not the page.

‹ Any gated action
Confirm your password
Role-gated
Almost every irreversible action asks for this first — confirming a purchase order, resolving a credit, creating an LTO, linking a count line, editing a par. Nine sections of this document mention it and none of them drew it. Eligibility is by role, not by level: a role without email auth gets “Step-up not available for your role” instead of a prompt, which is why the PIN is the primary credential below manager.
Confirm your password
Re-enter your password to confirm this action.
Password
••••••••
Wrong password.
Confirm
Cancel
Wrong password never locks you out here, and that is a deliberate decision the source states outright: you are already signed in, so locking an authenticated manager out of their own admin tools raises no real bar. Every failure is written to the audit log instead — forensics rather than friction.
Escape cancels this one, unlike the idle warning, because backing out of a destructive action is itself a safe outcome. A dead session is different again: it closes the modal and lets the route's own enforcement send you to the login screen, rather than showing a password error for a session that no longer exists.
The lockout banner still exists in this component defensively — the step-up route never locks, but the underlying account can already be locked from the login screen, and the modal would rather show a countdown than a confusing refusal.
‹ Opening · prep entry
Undo prep entry
Structured path
Undoing a saved prep count is silent if you just did it and structured if time has passed — and the client never guesses which. It tries the plain undo, and only opens this when the server refuses and asks for a reason.
Undo prep entry: Herb aioli
This entry was saved a while ago. Tell us why you're undoing it.
Reason
Re-enter the count
Other
Note
Required — explain why
Cancel
Undo entry
Other is selected, so the note is required and the confirm button is inert until something is typed — it renders in the disabled treatment rather than the danger outline it takes when submittable. Picking Re-enter the count makes the note optional and the button live immediately.
The reason the client never predicts the boundary is clock skew: a sixty-second edge decided locally would sometimes ask for a reason the server does not want, or skip one it does. Letting the refusal drive the modal is the honest version, and it is worth keeping.
It rises from the bottom on a phone and centres on a desktop, and tapping the backdrop cancels — safe, because nothing has happened yet. That is the opposite choice from the idle modal, for the opposite reason.
A wrong step-up password deliberately does not lock
The actor is already authenticated, so locking them out of admin raises no real bar — the source says so plainly. Failures go to the audit log instead. The lockout banner in the component is defensive only, for an account already locked from the login screen. Worth preserving: it is a considered decision that looks like an omission.
Escape means different things in different modals, correctly
Step-up and revoke both cancel on Escape, and revoke also cancels on a backdrop tap — because nothing has happened yet and backing out is safe. The idle warning ignores Escape entirely, because there the only safe outcome is an explicit choice. Three modals, two rules, and the difference is whether cancelling is itself an answer.
The revoke boundary is the server's to decide
A silent undo becomes a structured one after a delay, and the client never predicts where that line falls — clock skew on a sixty-second edge would make it wrong in both directions. It attempts the plain undo and reacts to the refusal. That pattern is worth naming in the spec as the house rule for any time-boxed permission.
Still owed at the time (six surfaces)
Three reports-hub detail views — cash, checklist and PM — plus ReportReferenceItem, PrepOverviewPanel and AddPrepItemForm. They are all read-and-draw work with no open questions — the honest reason they are not here is that this turn ran out of room, not that they are covered.

The chrome nobody designs

The last four surfaces, and the ones every employee touches without thinking about: the menu behind their initial, the login a manager uses, the modal that catches them at nine and a half minutes, and the search box that quietly finds more than it claims to. Every route and every component in the repo now has a pass.

The trigger is one initial in a circle, deliberately — the page header already prints the shop code and the person's name, and a second text affordance would crowd a phone. Everything global lives behind it.
This menu exists because operations pages used to be dead ends: no way back to the dashboard and no way to sign out, with a language toggle as the only global chrome. The Dashboard link hides itself when you are already there.
The Profile blurb only appears at AGM and up, and it is the one field a person writes about themselves anywhere in the app — it surfaces on their public profile. Language saves pessimistically: the toggle waits for the server's 200 before flipping, so a failed save never leaves a lie on screen.

Which field an error lands under is a decision, not an accident. A wrong password and an inactive account both sit under Password; an unverified email sits under Email, because that is the field you would go fix. Only the lockout gets the full-width banner, because it is the only one where waiting is the action.
The reset message is identical whether or not the address exists — a constant-shape response, so nobody can use this form to discover who works here. It also refuses to send without an email in the field above rather than silently doing nothing.
Password minimum is checked in the browser at eight characters before the request goes out, which saves a round trip and, more usefully, saves a failed-attempt count against a lockout.

0:23

Ten minutes of inactivity ends the session; this appears at nine and a half with thirty seconds on the clock. There is no way to dismiss it — Escape is ignored, the backdrop does nothing, and Tab cycles between the two buttons. An explicit choice is the whole design.
Activity listeners detach while it is open, so moving the mouse over the modal cannot silently reset the clock. The countdown is announced politely to screen readers rather than assertively, so it doesn't interrupt every second.
The server owns the real timeout and this only mirrors it. If the two drift, the next request 401s and the proxy redirects regardless of what this clock says — which is the right way round, but means a stale mirror shows a countdown that has already expired.

Two letters, three kinds of answer. People come first because a name is the most common thing anyone types, then pages as tappable chips, then the reports the box actually advertises — each of those a date with a type pill, who filed it, its status, and a badge for anything worth noticing. The people-and-pages block simply doesn't render when neither matches.
The page chips carry the current shop through the link, so tapping Maintenance Log from here lands on the right location instead of bouncing to the dashboard — the redirect 26a's back link had to work around.
Worth naming in the spec: the placeholder still says “Search name or type,” which undersells it. This box also reaches people and pages, and nobody would guess that from the field.
The user menu was a bug fix, and it shows
It began as a language toggle and grew a Dashboard link and Sign out only after someone noticed operations pages were dead ends. That history is why an identity menu holds a profile blurb editor: it is the one piece of global chrome, so anything global ends up in it. The name is UserMenu rather than LanguageSelector precisely so it can keep absorbing.
Error placement is the login's real design
Wrong password and inactive account both land under Password; an unverified email lands under Email — each error sits on the field you would go fix. Only the lockout takes a banner, because waiting is the action. And the reset reply is constant-shape either way, so the form can't be used to enumerate staff.
The idle modal cannot be dismissed, on purpose
Escape is ignored, the backdrop is inert, Tab cycles two buttons, and activity listeners detach while it is open so hovering can't reset the clock. The server owns the real ten minutes and this only mirrors it — correct, but it means a drifted mirror can show a countdown that already expired.
Search reaches further than its placeholder admits
It returns people and pages above the reports, and the page chips carry the current shop through so they land scoped rather than bouncing to the dashboard. The field still says “Search name or type”. Renaming it is a one-string change with an outsized effect on whether anyone finds a teammate here.
33a

Four more, all inherit-and-exception

The last of the operational islands, and they share a theme: each one exists to handle the line that doesn't fit. A count line pointing at nothing, a shop whose par differs from the company's, a prep row that is a question rather than a number. The general case is handled elsewhere; these are the exceptions made explicit.

Three states where a boolean would do, and the third is the useful one. Inherit global is not the same as On — it means this shop follows whatever the SKU says, so changing the global later still reaches it. A shop switched On stops listening.
Blank means inherit, and the placeholder says so rather than showing 0 — the same distinction the credits panel draws between an em dash and a zero. Setting every field back to inherit writes nulls instead of deleting the row, because the table is append-only.
Each shop saves on its own button and asks for a password first. Two shops, two saves — nothing here batches, which is the right call for a setting that quietly changes what a whole location orders.

A mixed section drops the shared header strip and gives each numeric row its own tiny caption instead, because two numeric lines in one section can carry different columns. The caption is marked decorative, because PrepRow already names every cell by section, item and column — without that, a screen reader would read the headings twice.
The yes-or-no row here is byte-identical to the Misc one on purpose. The comment in the source says the markup is duplicated rather than shared because the Misc row isn't exported — a real duplication risk worth naming in the spec, since the two must stay in lockstep by hand.
Linking preserves the line, not the label
The queue rewrites item_id or vendor_item_id on the line that already exists — same id, same wording. So a line called “Cambro of gravy” still reads that way after it points at Sunday Gravy. Fixing the label is a separate job in the builder, and the spec should say so or someone will expect the link to tidy it.
Three activation states, and the middle one is the point
“Inherit global” is not On. A shop left on inherit keeps following the SKU, so a later global change reaches it; a shop switched On has opted out permanently. Blank pars inherit too, and the placeholder says Inherit rather than showing a zero — the same em-dash-versus-zero discipline the credits panel uses.
Misc rows are attestations, so all four block submit
No column headers, nothing to total, and no partial credit: every yes-or-no must be answered before the form goes in. The error sits beside the toggle rather than in a summary at the top, which is the right place for a form someone fills standing up.
One row exists twice in the codebase by design
The mixed section replicates Misc's yes-or-no row verbatim because that row is module-private and can't be imported. The source comment is candid about it and asks for lockstep by hand. That is a genuine duplication to name in the handoff — the two will diverge the first time someone restyles a toggle.

Three terminal outcomes, one tap apart: Credit is money against the next invoice, Refund is money back, Write off is a decision to stop chasing it. None is reversible, so the buttons only appear after a first tap on Resolve — an inline confirm rather than a modal.
The damaged credit shows an em dash, not $0.00 — the amount genuinely isn't known until the vendor prices it. The written-off row shows a real $0.00, which means something different: it was priced, and it came to nothing. Conflating those two is how a shop loses track of what it's owed.
Every credit renders at any level; only AGM and up sees Resolve. The threshold is a mirrored constant in the client because the real one lives in a server-only module — the third such pair in this codebase, and the third that can drift.

The operator types in cases or eaches, and the ounces sit beside it either way — never instead of it. Ounces are what the recipes run on, so hiding them would train staff in a unit the system doesn't use. The stored value is always ounces; the typed unit is remembered only so the field reads back the way it was entered.
Typing 1.9 cases where the derivation said 2 is the whole point: the panel opens with the computed number and lets a person correct it. And a SKU with no ounce conversion loses its Case and Each toggles entirely — it can only be counted in ounces, which is the same unpriced-and-unlinked SKU family 10a surfaces.
An em dash and a zero mean different things
A credit with no amount yet renders —; a credit priced at nothing renders $0.00. The money law is stated in the component and it matters here more than anywhere: one is “we don't know what we're owed”, the other is “we're owed nothing”. Every other money surface in the app should be held to the same line.
Three mirrored gate constants now, all able to drift
CREDIT_RESOLVE_MIN 6 here, RECEIPT_MIN 4 and RECEIPT_OVERRIDE_MIN 6 in the claim panel — each duplicated into a client island because the real constant lives in a server-only module, each with a keep-in-sync comment. The build spec should name a single client-safe constants module rather than repeat the comment a fourth time.
Ounces are never hidden, only accompanied
The uses panel lets an operator work in cases or eaches, and prints the ounce equivalent beside every row regardless. Recipes run on ounces, so a UI that spoke only in cases would teach staff a unit the system doesn't hold. A SKU with no conversion simply loses the toggles.
The LTO list is a forecast, not a wish list
Its rows come from perishable surplus the catering pipeline already predicts — stock bought and unspoken for. That makes the deal reactive by construction, which is the model you described. A choice line greys out because there is no single item to attach an event to, and it says why rather than failing at submit.

This queue is the only place an unattributed receipt is visible. A scan that arrived with no shop and no order sits here until someone links it — and nothing anywhere else in the app counts it, so a forgotten row is a bill nobody is matching.
Two axes per row, and they move independently: which delivery a receipt belongs to, and which order it bills. Parse-now runs the extraction on demand, because the nightly sweep only touches emailed receipts — anything uploaded by hand waits for a tap.
Content type decides how a claim renders
An image or a PDF inlines from a private signed URL. Text, html and raw .eml get a link and nothing more — the rule is that vendor markup never enters our DOM, sandboxed or otherwise. A signed URL that fails to mint renders the filename with “unavailable” rather than a broken frame, which is the same null-leg honesty the three-way match uses.
Override is terminal, and only it needs a reason
Matches and Discrepancy are attestations a manager can revisit. Override is AGM-only, requires a written reason, and closes the question for good — the whole attestation bar is replaced by a line saying so. Two thresholds live in this file as mirrored constants (KH to see it, AGM to override) with a comment to keep them in sync with the server; that pair will drift.
The delivery axis and the order axis are separate
A receipt can be linked to a delivery, attached to a purchase order, both, or neither. The queue shows each independently, which is right — a receipt for goods that arrived on Monday may bill an order placed Thursday. It also means “linked” is ambiguous in conversation; the spec should always say linked to what.
Hand-uploaded receipts never parse themselves
The nightly sweep only reads emailed receipts, so anything scanned in waits for someone to tap Parse now. A failed parse is retryable and says so softly. Nothing schedules a retry, and nothing counts how many rows are sitting unparsed — the queue's own count says “3 waiting” about linking, not about reading.

Every label here comes from the people.* namespace, not the me.* one 9a uses — a distinction that matters, because 9a addresses the reader as the person being rated and this page addresses a manager reading about someone else. Two things worth keeping: the view carries a needs-work count the public profile is contractually forbidden from holding, and the score comes with a verdict in words. The AI slot ships empty and names itself, which beats hiding the section.
The audit is the anchor everything else drifts from
It is not a daily chore — the copy says to run it when the owner asks. Between audits, on-hand is inferred from deliveries, production and sales, and each row carries the provenance of its own number: Audited, Par-pass, or Inferred. That three-tier honesty is the best idea in the inventory half of this app and it appears nowhere else in the UI.
Two gap vocabularies, deliberately not one
A weighed SKU gets a variance, labelled short or over. Packaging has no consumption artifact, so it only gets “used or lost” — and when the count comes in high, the row says “counted over by 8 bag” instead of a signed number, because the sign convention is inverted between the two row types. Worth preserving verbatim; it is the kind of thing a rebuild flattens.
A silent data loss, now surfaced but not prevented
Submitting an audit drops any line that was started and not finished. A warning appears before you tap Record, and Record stays enabled — skipping a half-counted line is legitimate. But the warning names a count, not which lines, so the operator cannot check whether the drop is the one they meant.
“Order again” does not order again
On the customer account, that link routes to an empty builder — the reorder prefill is deferred in the source comment. It is the one label in the portal that promises something the click does not do, and it sits on the screen a repeat customer uses most.

Tuesday, in a paragraph
Sales landed close to a normal Tuesday, but two catering drops carried it — walk-in checks were down and the lunch rush started twenty minutes late. Comps ran high on sandwiches, all of them remakes, and two of the three name the same missed modifier. The drawer came up over, which usually means a comp was rung as a void.
Every clause here has to be traceable to an artifact, or it is a rumour with good grammar. The build should render each sentence with the record it leaned on.

alerts at ≥ 3%

+$57.85
The cash rule only fires on a shortfall, so an unexplained $57.85 over passes silently. Over and short are both drawer errors — worth making the rule symmetrical.

The recipe as the admin builder holds it — same record, so a change there reaches the line without anyone reprinting a binder. At 4× these read 8 qt, 12 cup, 24 ea, 8 tbsp.
Method
1
Pick and rough-chop the parsley. Stems out.
2
Zest two lemons, juice the rest. Strain the seeds.
3
Fold everything into the mayonnaise. Do not whip it.
4
Date and label. Five days, not six.
Photo slot — optional, one per step
These seven are proposals, not recreations
Every other turn in this document recreates a built surface. There is no UI behind any of these — each page renders one PlaceholderCard. What is real is the declared intent: each stub ships a title, a description and a feature list in both languages, and I built only from those. Where I invented past them — the batch scaler, the symmetric cash rule, the append-only correction — the frame says so.
A corrupted character sits in both languages
The AI thresholds read voids ?1.5%, comps ?3%, cash short ?$10 in en.json and again in es.json — a mojibaked ≥. It is user-visible today on the stub page. Worth a pass over the whole file for the same class of damage before any of it ships.
Some of these already exist in pieces
Three, in fact. Catering Insights has a read-only feedback panel, 7a designed the roll-up that Synthesis describes, and 8a already drew this recipe card. Building any of them from its own stub description would produce a duplicate — the spec has to name the existing surface first, which is why the frame above adds only a scaler.
Single-submission needs an escape
Prep locks on first submit, by design. But prep genuinely happens twice on a catering Tuesday, and the app has an idiom for exactly this — the append-only correction the overlay uses after its three-hour window. Reuse it rather than inventing a second unlock.

What changes at 390
The table becomes cards
Each line gets its own stepper at 44px. A phone keyboard over a numeric table is the worst version of this screen.
The cutoff clock stays visible
It is the only thing on the page with a deadline, so it pins to the top rather than scrolling away.
Place order and Save draft stack
Place is gold and primary; Save draft is the quiet escape for a count that is half done.
The reconcile gate contradicts its own documentation
The panel's header comment says AGM and up may mark an order reconciled. The code reads actorLevel >= 5, which is shift lead — two rungs lower. One of the two is wrong, and the comment is the one people will trust.
Confirm is also a save
Tapping Confirm patches any pending edit before confirming, so a quantity typed and never saved still lands in the frozen snapshot. Sensible — but “Save changes” sitting beside it implies the opposite, and the manager gets no confirmation that the unsaved number went in.
Automatic email is dormant everywhere
The outbound gate additionally requires a verified sending domain, which is the DNS errand still outstanding — so every store sees the dormant note and no one has ever seen the Send-to-vendor block. Inbound invoice parsing is a separate leg with no availability flag at all, which is why the billed column can only explain itself by naming the cadence.
An empty billed column has two meanings
No invoice has arrived, or one arrived after the last daily parse at about 5:45 AM. The panel says which only for an order already out the door, and it states the cadence rather than guessing about this invoice — the right call, and worth keeping when this gets rebuilt.

Two columns become one, the vendor and invoice fields collapse behind the PO banner, and the file bar pins to the bottom of the viewport rather than the page. Every tick stays 44px — the one measurement that cannot shrink, because it is hit with a thumb while holding a clipboard.
Three row states, three different rights
A confirmed row goes green with a white tick. An unconfirmed expected row shows a gold tick, because the tick is the whole job. The third state only exists on a shop with no template at all: an offered row, one of the vendor's own most-used SKUs, has nothing to accept — so it gets a dashed em-dash where the tick would be and reads “Tap to count.” It cannot appear here, because a PO prefill seeds every row with an expectation.
The suggested flag is dashed, not chosen
Count under expected and Short pre-selects itself in dashed outline with a dot, one tap from real. Nothing is filed off a suggestion — the operator still has to accept it, which is why the hint reads “Tap to confirm.”
A pre-filled count is a liability
The template seeds every row's quantity at what was ordered, so an item that never came off the truck files as fully received unless someone notices. That is the bug the gate exists for, and the gate is advisory — a second tap files anyway. Honesty, not a block.
A habit is not a debt
Shorts can only be claimed against a real order. When the prefill came from the vendor's last drop rather than a PO, the notice still appears but files nothing — “they usually bring this” is not something the vendor owes.
The pending-photo flag is free text
“Photo later” appends [PHOTO PENDING] to the note rather than setting a field, so nothing can reliably list deliveries still missing a receipt. One boolean column would make that queryable.
The draft is per shop, not per truck
One draft key per location. Two deliveries landing in the same hour share it, so starting the second offers to resume the first — and the resume banner shows only a time, not a vendor.

What each badge means
In progress
The door ceremony was started and never finished — someone walked away mid-count.
Discrepant
The two-way match found a difference between what the order said and what was counted.
Matched
Counted quantities agree with the purchase order. The only badge that is good news.
Overridden
A manager accepted the difference deliberately. Neutral, not settled — a decision is on record.
Photo missing
No receipt image attached. The paper is the fallback when a vendor disputes a count.
Missing email
Complete, never attested, no vendor claim on file, and older than 48 hours.
Three tones, and only Matched reads settled. Everything warn-toned is a thing a manager can still act on; the two neutral badges are states rather than problems.
Missing email is computed, not stored
A delivery earns that badge when four things are true at once: complete, still counted-only, no emailed claim, and past a 48-hour grace. The clock is read once per request, deliberately outside the render, so the flag can't drift mid-page. It means the badge appears on its own two days later with nobody doing anything.
Ordering and receiving name each other
Each page carries a link to the other in its header, and the active location travels in the URL so the destination resolves the same shop rather than bouncing to the dashboard. Draft, order, truck — one thread, two doors.
“{n} item(s)” again
The line count is another bracketed plural, so every row reads “6 item(s)”. Same wart as the quote builder's “1 line(s)” — worth fixing as one pass across both languages rather than one string at a time.

Before anything is drafted: a watermark rather than silence, and both cutoff vendors offering a draft. Tapping one disables every button on the card while it works, because two drafts for the same shop would race.
A cutoff vendor with a draft disappears from the queue
The Cutoff-today card only lists vendors with no draft yet — once one exists that vendor moves up into Today's orders instead. Two lists, one vendor, never both: the queue is work outstanding rather than a roster.
Six statuses, three tones
Draft and invoiced read neutral; confirmed is the single warn state; placed, received and reconciled all read settled. That means an order sitting confirmed — agreed but not sent — is the only thing on this surface that visually asks for a hand, which is the right choice.
The empty state is a watermark, not silence
Before the first draft the card shows the shared empty state — a decorative brand watermark above the message, here at 40px instead of its 64px default. The wording is “Nothing ordered yet today.” It replaced a card that rendered nothing at all, which read as a loading failure at 6am.
Drafting locks every button, not just its own
The generate handler disables the whole card while one request is in flight, so a manager can't start two drafts at once. Correct, but the other rows give no reason — they just stop working. A per-row spinner with the rest merely dimmed would say why.
The deep link is a fetch key, not a grant
A delivery detail can link back with ?po= and the panel opens on load. The id is untrusted by design: the panel's own fetch re-runs the level gate and the location lock server-side, so a crafted id renders a load error rather than another shop's order.
The history count is bare
Every other collapsible in the app passes a phrase — “14 SKUs”, “4 lines”. This one passes just the number, because its i18n value is literally {n}. Harmless, and the one inconsistency in the disclosure vocabulary worth normalising.
24a

The shelf walk that is the ordering system

The last built page with no design at the time, and the most phone-first thing in the app: a key holder walks the shelves and sets one number per SKU — how much to order to reach par. Vendors are collapsible, today's order day opens itself, and the whole walk resolves into draft orders per vendor. The page also mounts a second island — today's orders, PO history and cutoff attention — which is not drawn here. It became 25a. Written before those turns landed — 38a's card and the index carry the current answer.

Walk → review → recorded
One input per SKU and four one-tap chips around it. The distinction the whole design rests on: an empty field means not observed and never submits, while an explicit zero means the shelf is at par — recorded, ordering nothing.

Copy
Start a new walk
The PO code is the attribution key that travels in every transmitted body. Each method gets a row, its own action and its own Copy. The fourth has no navigable action on purpose: an address, URL or number that fails a conservative validator degrades to Copy-only rather than rendering a link built from an untrusted vendor value.
Empty and zero are different observations
A blank field is silence — that SKU was never walked, and no line is submitted for it. An explicit zero says the shelf is full: it records an on-hand anchor at par and orders nothing. The design makes them unmistakable, a blank stepper against a green field tagged full, because conflating them would either fabricate observations or lose them.
The two shelf extremes are one tap each
Empty · order 6 fills the full par for a bare shelf; We're full · 0 records par with nothing ordered. Suggest sits between them and only appears when there's an on-hand anchor to subtract from. A walker who taps nothing else can still finish a shelf in two taps per SKU.
A SKU with no weight can never earn a Suggest
Parsley has no order-unit-to-ounce conversion, so the system can't estimate what's on hand and the Suggest chip never renders. The row says so in muted text rather than leaving a blank — a chronic data gap to fix in SKU admin, not an incident. It's the same unpriced-SKU family 10a surfaces from the other side.
The blackout banner exists because it read as a bug
Before ~5 AM the nightly sales run hasn't landed, so estimates and Suggest chips are thin by design. The owner himself once read that silence as a regression, and the banner is the fix: it explains the gap in words and fabricates no number.
A failed PO doesn't lose the walk
If draft-order creation fails the observations still save, and the notice says so — the walk is the sacred record, the codes can be regenerated. That ordering of concerns is right, and it's the pattern the rest of the app should copy.
Shrinkage is advisory, deliberately
When a SKU moved more than sales explain, the post-walk notice names it and stops. No correction, no adjustment entry, no accusation — it hands a manager a question. Worth keeping that voice when the count-variance work lands.

23a

The first screen anyone sees

Two pages reached only from an email link, sharing one shell and one form. Both are dead ends by design when the link is wrong — and they part ways on what happens after success, which is the whole security argument between them.

Verify — a new employee's first minute
A mustard band with the wordmark, a focused column, two password fields. There is no back button and no sign-in link, because the only way here is the invitation email — and on success the API sets the session, so setting a password is signing in.

Operations
Network error. Check your connection.
Link not valid
This verification link is invalid or has already been used. Contact your manager.
← Back to sign in
Two failure shapes at once: a transient error as a five-second toast above the card, and the dead end that replaces the form entirely.
A bad link and no link read the same
The page checks the token against a 64-hex pattern before anything is sent, so a truncated paste and a used link both land on Link not valid — with different bodies, one telling you to open the email and one telling you to contact your manager. Nothing distinguishes expired from already-used, deliberately: the server keeps its response constant-shaped so a link can't be probed.
An inactive account fails at the password field
If the invitation is valid but the account has been deactivated, the error lands on the password input as “This account is inactive. Contact your manager.” It isn't a password problem, and putting it there makes it look like one. It belongs where the dead-end card is.
English only, before you have a language
Both pages force the translation provider to English, because a signed-out visitor has no stored preference. A Spanish-speaking new hire reads their very first screen in English — and every string here is already translated. The invitation email knows who it was sent to; the link could carry the language.
Reset — the same form, a different ending
Identical shell, identical fields, one deliberate difference: no automatic sign-in. A reset means someone may have lost control of the account, so every active session is revoked and the person signs in fresh.

Success is a card, not a redirect. The body says active sessions were signed out, which is the one place the app explains a security decision to the person it affects.
Reset says “expired”, verify never does
The reset dead end reads “invalid or has expired — request a new one from the sign-in page”, which gives a next action, and it is genuinely likely: a reset token lives one hour. Verify's equivalent says contact your manager, because an employee can't re-invite themselves. Two dead ends, two correct answers.
The success card is the only exit
There is no automatic redirect and no timer — the person clicks Sign in when they're ready. Right for a reset, and worth keeping: a password change is the last moment to bounce someone somewhere unexpected.
A password isn't the credential below manager
Floor staff sign in with a PIN, set by the manager who onboards them and matched to their Toast PIN so one number works on both. The password is supplemental — it secures the account rather than opening it — and only becomes the way in at manager level. That's why the reset route sends nothing below level 6: there is nothing to reset.
The gap is smaller than it looks, then, but it isn't nothing: a shift lead who finds this page and asks anyway gets a cheerful 200 and no email, because the constant response that blocks email enumeration also hides “you don't use one of these.” The sign-in page should say a forgotten PIN goes to a manager, and this page should never be reachable by someone who can't use it.

Checked before the form renders rather than on submit, so nobody counts a drawer into a box that would refuse it. The order of operations is the real rule: deposit before the closing is confirmed, or not at all.
Projected comes from Toast
The label says so outright, but it's typed by hand — the field is a number input, not a pull. The nightly Toast sync already lands the day's cash sales, so the one number a closer shouldn't have to transcribe is the one they do.
Anyone at the shop can be on shift
The checklist loads every active user at the location, not just managers, and a freeform row covers a trainee with no account yet. Those save with a null user id — a name on a record that can never be joined to a person.
The float is a constant
$200 is exported as a single shared constant and the hint states it as fact. A shop that runs a different float has no way to say so, and every deposit would be wrong by the difference. The server recomputes the totals with the same rule, so it wouldn't catch it either.
Maintenance Log
Fridge temperatures as a fourteen-day trend line with the safe maximum dashed across it, equipment in a two-up grid, and a note form that follows you between views. One page, two states, switched by a query param rather than a route. The prep cooler shows the shape worth noticing: a temperature and a trend, with “No reading today” beside them — the last reading is known, it just isn't from today.

Ten readings over the line, and nobody was told
The status is computed on read, so it's correct the moment someone opens this page — and silent until then. A fridge above 41°F is exactly the class of event the notification system already handles for under-par prep; this one raises nothing.
“Other…” logs against nothing
Picking it saves the note with a null equipment id and whatever name was typed. That's the right escape hatch for a broken thing nobody registered — but the note then belongs to no unit, so it appears on no detail page and in no history. Those notes are only ever seen once.
A note with no author came from a checklist
When a temperature note is captured during closing rather than typed here, it lands with no user and the row says from checklist instead of a name. Good instinct — and it means the two paths into this log are visibly different.
A below-level view says so
Below level 3 this page renders “Maintenance Log is not available for your role” instead of bouncing to the dashboard — the only gated surface in the app that explains itself rather than redirecting. It's the better pattern, and it's used once.
Settings
Deliberately thin, and honest about it: one real preference, a link to the page that owns identity, and a card that admits notification preferences aren't built. The restraint is the design decision worth keeping.

Two radio buttons, and the choice only commits after the server confirms — so both are disabled while the write is in flight, which is the state drawn here alongside the Saving… line. It changes every string in the app including the food labels a prep lead prints. Everything else a person might expect here has no schema, so the page doesn't pretend.
The card that can't be honest much longer
Notification preferences aren't missing — the table exists and the send path already honours per-user channels, so a row can say SMS-only today with no way to set it. That's why a manager can silently receive nothing. This card and 18a's bell are the same gap seen from both ends.
Settings links rather than duplicates
Identity lives on the profile page, and this page sends you there instead of copying the fields. Worth preserving as the pattern when notification prefs land: one owner per concept.

The processing result is the useful column. unmapped_location means a real order arrived for a shop whose EZCater UUID isn't filled in above — it was logged and dropped. invalid_signature means something posted to our webhook that couldn't prove it was EZCater — and that row carries no event key or order id, because a body we can't verify is never parsed for either.
A dropped order looks like a log line
An order for an unmapped shop is recorded and discarded — no lead, no notification, nothing on a dashboard. The only place it exists is this list, on a tab nobody opens daily. That row deserves to raise something.
Only one of these brings orders in
EZCater does. A signed webhook arrives, the caterer UUID above resolves it to a shop, the order is fetched and written as a pipeline lead with the platform's order id on it — which is how the EZCater leads on 15a's board got there without anyone typing them. A cancellation cancels the lead; a repeat of the same order id is ignored as a duplicate.
Toast doesn't. The crosswalk is a menu mapping: it ties our items to their item ids so the nightly sales pull can be read as our own products — the velocity band in 6a and the sales tab in 17a. Counter sales come in; catering orders don't.
Room for a third costs a migration
Each platform is currently its own column on the locations row, its own save route and its own intake module. Adding Grubhub means another column, another route, another parser — and this tab grows a third hard-coded field.
The shape that generalises: one link table keyed by shop, platform and external id, with a role on each row saying whether that platform sends orders, sales, or both. Then the tab renders a list, the Add slot is real, and a new platform is an adapter rather than a schema change.
Two ID fields, no validation shown
Both save buttons stay disabled until you type, then accept anything — the GUID and UUID are checked server-side, so a malformed value comes back as an error rather than being caught in the field. A format hint next to each would cost nothing.
Drift is a button, not a watch
Nothing checks for drift on a schedule. A price that diverged in March stays undetected until someone happens to press this. The nightly Toast pull already runs — a drift pass on the same cron, surfacing to the admin hub, is the obvious next step.

Portions
“Portions” is the piece model
That third toggle is what lets a sub be split into pieces — the unit every package in 19a counts in. All three are on here, and they have to be: each one is an eligible option on a platter or a box. Turn one off and nothing downstream notices: the package picker filters on catering available and never on this flag, so the editor still offers that sub as a platter option and a manager can build a platter out of a sub the kitchen isn't allowed to halve. The two disagree silently, and the platter is the one that ships.
Edit catering packages →
Only implies available
Turning Only on turns Catering on too — the server enforces it and the page redraws from what came back. That's the Assorted cans row: catering-only, so it never appears on the counter menu.
Serves lives in two places
The item carries a serves figure, blank meaning one, and each size carries its own. A single can leaves the item blank, so it reads as one; its Case of 24 size carries the 24. A 32 oz pan serves 12 the same way. This is the number every coverage bar in the customer flow counts against, which is why putting a case's figure on the item would inflate the drinks bar twenty-fourfold.
Two ways to price a size
A size takes an explicit dollar price here, while 17a's rate rules derive a catering price from the menu price. Two mechanisms produce the same number and neither editor mentions the other — worth settling which wins before a manager sets both.

Five fields, and the location picker is the one that only appears here — on an existing row it isn't rendered at all, so a global question can never be narrowed to one shop. English question and answer are required; the Spanish halves save as empty rather than blocking, which is how a row ends up half-translated.
Key and order are visible and unreachable
Each row prints its key and its display order, and the list sorts by that order — but the form collects neither. Its payload is a location and four strings, on create as well as on edit, so both fields are set once by the server and are unreachable from the app forever after. Reordering the FAQ means editing the database. A drag handle, or even a number field, is a small addition with an obvious payoff.
Deactivating keeps the answer
The tip question is retired rather than deleted, because the storefront still links to it by key. Retiring is Tier B; editing the words is Tier A — the same inversion the packages editor has, where changing what a customer reads is cheaper than hiding it.
19a

What we sell, and how much of it

Two editors from the catering hub I'd only drawn as doors. Packages is a disclosure list with choice slots and price advice; Capacity sets the ceilings and the days we don't cater. Between them they explain a signal three turns away.

Catering Packages
Every package is a piece count and a list of what the customer may choose — a piece being half a sub. A platter comes in 32, 16 or 8 pieces; a lunch box is one or two pieces plus chips and a drink. Pieces and covers aren't the same number — a 32-piece platter is sixteen subs and feeds 24, because people take more than one piece. The builder sets the approved list; the storefront lets the customer pick from it.

A piece is half a sub
The unit is a piece, and a sub is two of them. So 32 pieces is sixteen subs, 16 is eight, 8 is four — and because a sub can't be split across two varieties, every variety a customer picks arrives as at least two pieces. Setting a package means choosing the piece count; everything else follows from it.
It holds for the boxes too. A full lunch box is two pieces, one whole sub; a light box is one piece. Every package in the list is the same build at a different number.
The builder can't say “pairs”
A choice slot stores one number, and the source renders it as “pick 32” — so the screen says a customer makes thirty-two choices when they make sixteen. Nothing records that pieces come in pairs of one variety.
Worth building: store the piece count, derive the sub count beside it, and have the storefront picker allocate in multiples of two. The gold note on the slot above is that derived line, which the app doesn't show today.
A piece count priced as a unit count
Price advice multiplies the line quantity by a per-item price. Give it 32 pieces and prices that are per whole sub, and it returns $500.05 — double the truth — then reports the $285.00 platter as a 43% discount when it is really a 14% premium.
The same fault is why a lunch box's two-piece slot prices as two whole subs. Fixing the pairing model fixes the pricing: pieces divided by two, times the average of the eligible subs.
A package can't contain a package
A line references an item or a menu item, mutually exclusive, with no third option — so a spread that wants a platter inside it has to re-list the platter's contents, and drifts the moment the platter changes.
Worth building: let a line reference a package and resolve it recursively, so price advice and prep demand both see through it. Quote lines already carry a package id; only package lines can't.
Repricing asks for less than hiding
Editing a package's fields — price included — is a Tier A step-up. Creating one and deactivating one are Tier B. So moving $285 to $28 is the cheaper action, which is backwards for the one field that takes money.
Location is permanent
Slug and location are identity fields and the edit request drops them, so a Capitol Hill platter can never become global — which is why the three platter sizes are three rows and the two boxes are global. The only way to move one is to deactivate it and build it again.
Capacity & Blackouts
One card per location: three caps that can each be left blank, and the dates the shop won't cater. This is where 15a's “limited availability” pill comes from — and where its silence comes from too, because a shop with no caps set can never be too busy.

Where the pipeline pill comes from
Capitol Hill's 400-cover ceiling is what makes 15a's Sep 3 lead read Limited availability · 55 covers left — 55 of 400 sits under the 15% mark where the signal changes. Set the cap to 120 and the same day reads differently; leave it blank and the lead says nothing at all.
Two lead times, no conversation
A location has a minimum lead time and so does every package. Navy Yard asks 48 hours; Full Lunch Box asks 24. Nothing reconciles them, so a 24-hour package on a 48-hour shop is a promise the storefront can make and the kitchen can't keep. Whichever is stricter should win, and it should be visible on both editors.
Nothing here blocks an order
Caps produce an advisory signal on the pipeline card, not a refusal. A blackout is the same — removing one deactivates rather than deletes, so the record survives, but a lead can still be booked onto Christmas Day. If these are meant to be gates, that decision hasn't been made; right now they're labels.

Alerts, and the one thing we print

Two surfaces that only exist to tell someone something. The bell carries alerts a manager has to act on before service, and the label sheet is the app's single printed artifact — a safety document where a missing allergen has to look like a missing allergen.

The bell, open
Always visible, badge only when something is unread, and the card is the read surface — tapping one marks it read and it leaves the list. There's no drill-through, because every field a manager needs was written into the notification at emit time.

Why the third card has no body
The card only builds a detail block for an under-par alert; every other type falls through to title and timestamp. The opening-with-no-prior-data alert has a long, carefully written body string in both languages — who opened, the attested cause, how many items were recounted — and none of it renders. Cross-day cards say so
Today's alerts read CAP · 9:42 AM; anything from a previous operational day gains a date, as the third card does. The comparison runs in New York time, not the browser's, so a manager checking from the west coast still sees the shop's day.

Notifications

The bell shows unread only
There is no read history here — the loader filters to unread, so a card tapped by accident is gone from every surface in the app. Nothing lists what you dismissed. Archival reading is slated for a later Reports Hub, which means today the bell is the only copy.
It doesn't update while you watch
The count is rendered with the dashboard and refreshed by the mark-read write. Nothing polls, and the notifications API answers every request with “not implemented.” An alert raised at 9:42 reaches a manager who left the tab open at 9:00 whenever they next reload.
Three channels, one that arrives
Recipients can be marked for in-app, SMS or email, and per-user preferences are honoured when the notification is written. But the bell reads in-app rows only, and the preferences screen says they're “coming in a follow-up” — so a manager whose row was written as SMS-only currently gets nothing at all, silently.
The label sheet
A safety artifact, and the only screen in the app designed to be printed and stuck to a pan. Its governing rule is that absence is never rendered as safe. Everything past that rule is a proposal — today the page prints one fixed two-up rectangle per quote line, with no stock, shape, granularity, logo or reprint.

The setup behind the money

Two money pages, a fourteen-day prep read, and two editors that both call themselves zones. Rates decide what an item costs; Pricing decides what gets added on top. The worked example reproduces the Brightline quote to the cent, so you can see which knob moves what.

The other money page
Catering prices are derived, not typed — a rate is applied to the item's regular menu price. Rates resolve most specific first: an item override beats its section, which beats the location default. Each input takes a percentage or a target price and shows you the other one.

Two rate pages, two meanings
This page sets what an item costs. Pricing & Tax sets what gets added on top — tax, gratuity, service charge, deposit. Both are level 8, both are called rates in conversation, and the hub gives them adjacent cards with no hint which is which.
A rate change is retroactive
Removing a rate doesn't restore the old price — it falls back to the next tier up, which may be higher or lower. Existing quotes are safe because they carry their own snapshot, but nothing on this page shows what the next quote will cost.
Where the charge stack comes from
One card per location, each holding exactly one active rule — a partial-unique index enforces that, so this is a form and not a list. Collapsed, a card is a single line of rates; the fields only appear when you edit. Rates store as basis points and the server recomputes them from your percentage.

The Brightline quote in 16a, to the cent. The tax base is food plus the service charge plus delivery: the service charge is always taxed, and delivery is taxed because this location's tax on delivery flag is on.
Two things the flags don't cover
There's a toggle for taxing delivery and one for taxing gratuity, but none for the service charge — it is unconditionally in the tax base. That's the common jurisdiction, and it's a deliberate choice in the math rather than an oversight; it just isn't a choice this page offers.
Nothing here is dated, but quotes are protected anyway: every quote snapshots the rates it was computed with, so changing 10.00 here reprices only quotes built afterwards. What it does silently change is the counter-facing charge on new orders, with no record of when the number moved.
Managing every location's pricing takes level 9 — Owner. A Manager of Operations at 8 edits only the locations assigned to them, which is tighter than the rest of the app, where 7 already grants all-locations access.
Fourteen days of prep, before it's prep
Four tabs over one location and one fixed window. Prep is what to make, Raw / SKU is what it consumes, Surplus is what will be left, and Sales is the Toast pull. Read-only throughout — the only way out is a link to the pars page.

The money surface and the identity model behind it. The builder borrows the customer flow's two-column shape — lines on the left, a live total and the coverage read on the right — and drops everything that was there to sell. Nothing here computes a price: the server answers, the page displays.

When a quote changes
A revision is a new version, not an edit — and it lands as a draft, not a send. Someone has to send v3 before the customer sees anything, which is a step easy to forget after a phone call about adding a platter. Only what moved is shown, with its price, because a customer re-reading twenty unchanged lines is how a change slips past someone.

One page, four origins
Every catering order opens on the quote page regardless of where it came from — same lines, same stack, same payment record. What differs is what the page will let you do, and the page says which one it is rather than hiding the difference.
Where it came from, and what that costs you
Self-serve portal
built by the customer
Opens fully. The customer holds the link, so a revision re-review goes straight back to them and the deposit is already recorded against the order.
Nothing withheld.
Staff quote
built at the shop
Opens fully, and this is the origin the builder produces. Send, revise, mark paid, print labels.
Nothing withheld — but the customer only ever sees the versions you send.
Marketplace · ezCater
booked off-platform
Opens read-mostly: lines, coverage, prep, labels. What we book and what they paid are both on the record.
No revise, no send, no deposit — pricing and payment belong to the platform. Changes go through their portal or they don't happen.
Phone or walk-in
typed in after the fact
Opens fully once a customer email exists. Without one it's an internal record: lines and prep work, labels print.
No send until someone has an address to send to. Deposit is marked by hand, which is the check-or-cash case.
Today only staff quotes have this page, so an ezCater order lives in the pipeline as a card with a price and nothing behind it. Making one page serve all four is what lets a shift lead answer “what's in the Friday order” without knowing which system booked it.
The quote itself
What a quote looks like once it exists: the snapshot, its lines, the stack, and the payment intents underneath. Sending needs a password re-entry — a quote leaving the building is the one action here that reaches a customer.

Two errors this panel exists to say out loud

15a

The catering side of the house

Everything 14a books has to land somewhere a person works it. This is that place: a board of leads, a directory of who they belong to, and one read that says whether catering is making money. All four screens are drawn from source, including the stage vocabulary and the capacity signals.

The board
Six stages, not five — Out for delivery sits between Confirmed and Completed, which is the stage a shift lead actually looks for at 10am. Search replaces the board rather than filtering it, because a phone call needs a phone number, not a column.

14a

The customer ordering flow

The storefront is already good, so it stays as it is. What needed work is the funnel behind it — the four screens between “start your order” and an order on the record. All four are drawn from source now, including the coverage guide that answers the headcount question before anyone has to ask it. The one thing here that isn't in the code is the print action on step four, flagged where it sits.

Step one · who and where
An intake form, not a cart — and no password anywhere. The address is checked against the delivery zones on the spot, so a customer learns which shop is making it before they invest any time. Then a one-time link lands in their inbox.

10a

The spine — SKUs, items, pars

You called these the connecting pages, and the code already has the concept that connects them: readiness. A SKU isn't ready until its pack resolves to ounces and it has a price; an item isn't ready until its SKUs are. So the design job is showing what's incomplete, why, and which record upstream is the actual cause.

9a

The people surfaces

These needed care rather than polish, and the source already decided most of it. My Performance is own-data-only with manager notes never selected and deliberately no rank. Written Reports is append-only, authorable by any employee, and carries a visibility floor. Neither is a discipline system, so neither should look like one.

My Performance
A plain-language read, one score it explains rather than hides, and wins as pills. No rank, no needs-attention list — and it says out loud that the manager's private note isn't here, because otherwise people assume it is.

Marketplace orders arrive with a headcount, a handoff time, and the gap between what the customer paid and what you keep. In-house orders don't — which is the honest reason to label the source on every row. Separately, Toast stamps every order with a dining option, and the captured payload shows a catering one alongside dine-in and takeout — so catering rung through the register can be split out too, without the platform.
Correction on the velocity view: I said the clock times were already in your Toast payload and being discarded. They are not. The captured ordersBulk fixture carries only businessDate as a bare integer date — orders and checks have guid, voided, dining option and selections, and no time of day anywhere. Toast's API documents order timestamps, but nothing in the repo proves they come back on this call, and this codebase has been burned by that assumption before. So: confirm against a live payload first. If the times are there, it is a field on the sale line plus a column. If not, hourly and daypart need a different endpoint, and this panel should wait.

The same app on a laptop

Today every page is max-w-2xl → xl:max-w-6xl — one centered column that just gets wider, so a 1512px screen shows phone-shaped cards floating in empty margins. Receiving already proves the better pattern with its lg:grid-cols-[3fr_2fr] rail. This applies that everywhere: the width buys a persistent sidebar and a reference rail, not bigger whitespace.

Dashboard · 1280 and up
Grouped nav leaves the content column and becomes a sidebar. The hero stays one dominant action; the right rail takes what was below the fold on the phone.

The rule at each width
Phone · under 640
One column, nav grouped at the bottom, hero first. Targets stay 48px+ and nothing sits under a thumb-blocked edge.
Tablet · 640–1023
Hero stays full width; tiles and nav groups go two-up. Counter tablets keep the phone's target sizes — same wet hands.
Laptop · 1024+
Nav leaves the content and becomes a sidebar. Main splits roughly 60/40 — work on the left, reference on the right, like Receiving already does.
Desktop · 1440+
Content caps around 1400 and centers. Extra width goes to the rail, never to text — body copy stays under 75 characters.
